claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs is governed by Al-induced chemical short-range ordering.
Al-induced chemical short-range ordering locally distorts the FCC lattice.
Al-induced ordering destabilizes the single-phase FCC state and produces an ordered B2 or similar precipitate phase.
An ordered precipitate phase can mediate transformation-assisted strengthening.
A low-Al Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy is a single-phase, disordered FCC solid solution.
Increasing Al content or applying ordering-promoting aging treatments forms nanoscale B2 or other ordered intermetallic precipitates in an FCC matrix.
Ordered precipitates generate local stress fields that hinder defect mobility.
Hindering defect mobility with ordered precipitates improves radiation tolerance by trapping irradiation-induced defects or cascades.
The ordered precipitates improve high-temperature strength.
Ordered B2-like precipitates serve as sites for transformation-induced plasticity.
A moderate increase in Al content will produce detectable ordered precipitates coexisting with FCC.
A moderate increase in Al content will increase high-temperature yield strength and hardness relative to the low-Al FCC baseline.
The ordered-precipitate microstructure will reduce the accumulation of irradiation-induced defects.
The ordered-precipitate microstructure will enhance cryogenic toughness through activated transformation mechanisms.
The proposed Al modification will retain environmental resistance.
The hypothesis applies in an Al concentration window likely below approximately 20 at.%.
At higher Al contents, excessive ordering may cause brittleness or a complete phase transformation that eliminates the desired property combination.
Failure of increasing Al content to form an ordered phase, or failure of that phase to correlate with the specified property improvements, would falsify the hypothesis.
